title: AI Agents for Performance: Ship Faster, Pay Less — Rajat Shah, Netflix

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is the architecture of an AI agent system that automates performance engineering: a defined loop (read profiling data, identify anti-patterns, search code, locate method, produce fix, validate with canary, send code review), a harness integrating profiling tools, Git repos, code search, and canary deployment, and a stepwise autonomy model (Levels 0 to 3). The agent system design—including scheduled continuous runs, tool integration points, and the control plane—is the core subject, not any single tool or workflow engine. Evidence: the speaker explicitly states 'this talk mainly covered the level two orchestration' and describes harnesses, hooks, integrations, and scheduled weekly runs as the Level 2 focus.

secondary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
secondary.rationale: The agent's primary output is code reviews and performance fixes in production codebases. The shift-left strategy explicitly envisions feeding the pattern catalog into coding agents during code authoring to prevent anti-patterns before they ship. Cross-repo code search and checking out repos at production commits are integral to the agent workflow, and the talk frames coding agents as both the source of the problem (fast but non-performant code) and part of the solution (feeding patterns to them).

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: The centralized pattern catalog is explicitly described as 'long-term memory' for stateless LLM agents, addressing their compact memory limitation. The catalog structure—queryable hints, symbols, confidence levels, and anti-pattern/good-pattern pairs—is engineered to fit within agent context windows and provide durable, reusable state across invocations and services. The speaker contrasts a stateful catalog with a stateless LLM to create fleet-wide memory.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: Canary validation serves as a prerequisite evaluation gate: the agent compares old vs new code on real production traffic for approximately 10 minutes, measuring CPU, latency, and error rates. Confidence levels in the pattern catalog increase as more services validate a finding, creating a measurement-driven trust mechanism before human review.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The agent system is developer infrastructure for performance engineering at Netflix, integrating profiling, code search, Git, and canary deployment into a platform that other engineering teams use to identify and fix performance issues across services.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The talk describes an internal enterprise workflow for performance engineering and infrastructure cost optimization at Netflix, with scheduled continuous profiling runs and cross-service pattern detection across the organization's service fleet.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The agent produces code reviews and the shift-left strategy envisions feeding the pattern catalog into coding agents during code authoring, making it directly relevant to IDE and PR-assistant workflows.

summary: Rajat Shah, Staff Software Engineer at Netflix's AI Platform org, presents a practitioner's playbook for integrating AI agents into performance engineering for ML model serving infrastructure. The core problem: coding agents produce code roughly 10x faster but optimize for writing speed rather than runtime performance, driving up compute costs. Shah's team built an agent that reads structured profiling data (call stacks with self/inclusive CPU metrics), identifies anti-patterns, searches source code across repositories, and produces validated fixes. Key results include identifying a quadratic-time pattern (immutable map copy in a tensor merge method) consuming 8.8% CPU and completing the full find-to-code-review cycle in under 5 minutes, plus detecting a spectator-metrics counter allocation pattern across 7 services with 0.5–4.6% potential CPU savings. To address LLMs' limited context memory, Shah introduces a centralized pattern catalog stored as markdown files in a Git repo—intentionally not a vector database—containing queryable hints, symbols, confirmed services, confidence levels, and anti-pattern/good-pattern pairs. Before human review, fixes must pass functional tests and canary validation (~10 minutes on real traffic comparing CPU, latency, and error rates). The mental model: profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, engineer makes the decision. Shah outlines a stepwise autonomy model: Level 0 (manual), Level 1 (LLM identification), Level 2 (orchestration with tools, integrations, scheduled weekly runs), and Level 3 (autonomous planning requiring heavy security investment). He recommends starting at Level 1 and moving to Level 2 for maximum benefit. Foundations—test coverage, canary automation, integration points—must be solid before layering AI agents.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a complete production agent system for performance engineering that addresses the full lifecycle from problem creation to validated fix. The talk's central insight is a feedback loop: coding agents create performance debt (coding agents as source of performance debt), which is then detected by an orchestrated agent reading profiling data (LLM-based anti-pattern recognition, performance profiling), persisted in a shared catalog for fleet-wide learning (pattern catalog as long-term memory, stateless LLM with stateful external memory, confidence-based escalation), validated through real-traffic experiments (canary deployment, A/B validation), governed by a stepwise maturity model (agent autonomy levels), and ultimately fed back to prevent future occurrences (shift-left strategy, context window management). The software engineering concepts (profiling, canary, test coverage, cross-repo search, Git commit identification) provide the infrastructure that the AI concepts (orchestration, autonomy levels, security guardrails, catalog memory) operate on top of. Together they demonstrate how to build an agent that identifies, fixes, and validates performance problems in production ML serving infrastructure while maintaining human control and accumulating organizational knowledge over time.
temporalContext: The video was published on July 28, 2026, recorded at AI Engineer World's Fair SF 2026. The talk describes a system that was in production at Netflix as of mid-2026, as confirmed by the WeAreDevelopers session page stating 'This is not a demo. This is already in production at Netflix.' The speaker's LinkedIn post on July 30, 2026 confirmed specific canary results (-6.5% CPU, -3% p90 latency). A related talk was scheduled for WeAreDevelopers World Congress 2026 NA (September 23–25, 2026), indicating continued development and evolution of the system. The Netflix Tech Blog post on ML model serving (May 2026) co-authored by the speaker confirms the Model Inference Platform's scale at 1M+ requests per second. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026, approximately 25 days after the video was published.
takeaways: AI coding agents produce code fast but not always performant—compute costs rise alongside code production speed because agents lack platform-specific knowledge

A centralized pattern catalog in a Git repo serves as long-term memory for stateless LLM agents, eliminating the need for vector databases at the start; humans can also author patterns when building new frameworks
Human approval remains critical—the agent sends code reviews, not direct production pushes, because modifying running production code without business context is risky

Canary validation on real traffic is a prerequisite before human review: two machines, ~10 minutes, comparing CPU, latency, and error rates; profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, engineer makes the final decision
The shift-left strategy moves from reactive production fixes to proactive inline review comments and ultimately to feeding the catalog into coding agents during code authoring

Foundations—test coverage, canary automation, business logic tests—must be solid before layering AI agents on top; invest in integration points (profiling triggers, data download, canary invocation) before introducing the LLM

A stepwise autonomy model applies: Level 0 manual, Level 1 LLM for identification, Level 2 orchestration with tools and scheduled runs, Level 3 agent plans and reasons but requires heavy security investment
Start with the reactive path (not a bad approach) and gradually move left toward proactive prevention; Level 2 yields maximum benefit for most teams
Weekly scheduled agent runs on services continuously identify newly introduced performance problems, keeping identification close to when code was written

concepts.name: Agent autonomy levels (0–3)
concepts.explanation: A stepwise model for AI agent autonomy: Level 0 is fully manual, Level 1 introduces an LLM for identification only, Level 2 adds orchestration with tools/integrations/harnesses/hooks and scheduled runs, Level 3 gives the agent capabilities to plan, reason, and act autonomously but requires heavy security investment.
concepts.importance: Provides a practical framework for teams to incrementally adopt AI agents in performance engineering, with clear guidance on when to advance and what prerequisites each level demands.

concepts.name: Agent orchestration with tool integration
concepts.explanation: Level 2 autonomy involves integrating tools, harnesses, hooks, and integrations into the agent loop for profiling triggers, profiling data download, code search, canary invocation, and report generation.
concepts.importance: The orchestration layer is the focus of the talk and represents the level where teams get maximum benefit—connecting the LLM to real infrastructure tools.

concepts.name: Stateless LLM with stateful external memory
concepts.explanation: Combining a stateless LLM agent with a stateful pattern catalog (markdown files in Git) to create fleet-wide memory that persists across invocations, services, and time.
concepts.importance: This architecture pattern addresses the fundamental limitation of LLMs having compact memory and enables accumulated knowledge to benefit future agent runs.

concepts.name: LLM-based anti-pattern recognition from profiling data
concepts.explanation: LLMs trained on quality code can recognize common performance anti-patterns—such as O(N²) loops, loop invariants, repeated allocation, and batching issues—directly from structured profiling data without first scanning the codebase.
concepts.importance: This is the key insight that makes the entire approach viable: the LLM serves as a pattern matcher on profiling data, dramatically reducing the time from profiling to identification.

concepts.name: Agent security guardrails and prompt injection risks
concepts.explanation: Level 3 autonomy—where agents plan, reason, and act without human approval—requires heavy investment in evaluation, sandboxing, and security guardrails against prompt injection and other attacks that agent infrastructure cannot currently fully solve.
concepts.importance: Defines the boundary of safe autonomous operation and explains why the talk recommends stopping at Level 2 for most teams.

concepts.name: Coding agents as source of performance debt
concepts.explanation: AI coding agents produce code roughly 10x faster than before but lack platform-specific knowledge and may invent suboptimal patterns, creating non-performant code that increases compute costs.
concepts.importance: Frames the problem the talk addresses: the same AI that accelerates development also creates the performance problems the agent system is designed to catch.

concepts.name: Context window management for agent catalogs
concepts.explanation: The pattern catalog must be hierarchically structured and indexed to avoid filling agent context windows unnecessarily, ensuring the agent receives only relevant patterns for a given profiling finding.
concepts.importance: Without careful catalog design, the agent's context window fills with irrelevant patterns, degrading its ability to produce accurate findings.

concepts.name: Confidence-based escalation for agent findings
concepts.explanation: Pattern catalog entries include confidence levels that increase as more services validate a finding, helping future agents decide whether a finding is worth sending for human review.
concepts.importance: Creates a measurement-driven trust mechanism that reduces false positives and focuses human reviewers on high-confidence findings.

concepts.name: Performance profiling and call stack analysis
concepts.explanation: Using structured profiling data with self CPU and inclusive CPU metrics to identify runtime bottlenecks. The talk's core premise is that all profilers output universally parseable call stack data, making it suitable for direct LLM consumption.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational input to the entire agent pipeline—without structured profiling data, the agent cannot identify anti-patterns or trace them to source code.

concepts.name: O(N²) quadratic-time anti-patterns
concepts.explanation: Algorithms with quadratic complexity causing disproportionate CPU usage. The talk's primary example is an immutable map copy inside a tensor merge method consuming 8.8% of CPU during profiling.
concepts.importance: This is the concrete anti-pattern the agent successfully identified, demonstrating the value of automated profiling analysis over manual inspection.

concepts.name: Canary deployment and A/B traffic validation
concepts.explanation: Deploying new code alongside old code on separate machines receiving identical traffic for approximately 10 minutes to measure CPU, latency, and error rate differences before promoting changes to production.
concepts.importance: Canary validation is the prerequisite evaluation gate before human review, providing ground-truth performance data rather than relying on model confidence alone.

concepts.name: Cross-repository code search
concepts.explanation: Searching across multiple service repositories to find instances of the same anti-pattern, enabling fleet-wide remediation. The agent found a spectator-metrics counter allocation pattern repeated across 7 different services.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that agent-driven code search can surface systemic patterns invisible to individual teams, with potential CPU savings of 0.5–4.6% across affected services.

concepts.name: Shift-left strategy for performance engineering
concepts.explanation: Moving performance validation earlier in the development cycle: from reactive production fixes to proactive inline code review comments to ultimately feeding the pattern catalog into coding agents during code authoring.
concepts.importance: This strategy connects reactive fixes to proactive prevention, reducing the cost and risk of performance problems by catching them closer to when code is written.

concepts.name: Test coverage as a prerequisite for AI-driven optimization
concepts.explanation: Solid unit and integration tests must exist before AI agents propose performance changes, as agents need functional correctness verification before optimization changes are safe to canary and review.
concepts.importance: Without test coverage, the agent cannot verify that performance fixes do not break business logic, making this a hard prerequisite for deploying the system.

concepts.name: Pattern catalog as long-term memory for agents
concepts.explanation: A centralized repository of performance patterns and anti-patterns stored as markdown files in a Git repo—intentionally not a vector database—serving as durable, queryable memory for stateless LLM agents across invocations and services.
concepts.importance: Solves the LLM compact memory problem by creating fleet-wide memory through a stateful catalog combined with a stateless LLM, enabling pattern reuse and confidence escalation.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-loop code review
concepts.explanation: The agent produces code reviews rather than pushing directly to production, maintaining human judgment for business context, risk assessment, and final approval decisions.
concepts.importance: Ensures that risky production code changes are always reviewed by engineers who understand business context that the agent lacks.

concepts.name: Git-based production commit identification
concepts.explanation: Checking out the exact production commit to ensure the agent's analysis, code search, and fix proposals match the deployed code rather than a different branch or version.
concepts.importance: Ensures that proposed fixes target the actual production code, making the agent's output actionable and accurate for code review.

concepts.name: Scheduled continuous profiling runs
concepts.explanation: Weekly scheduled agent runs on services to continuously identify newly introduced performance problems, keeping identification close to when code was written.
concepts.importance: Enables proactive detection of regressions introduced by new code, rather than waiting for manual profiling during incidents.

sections.title: Introduction and problem framing
sections.summary: Rajat Shah introduces himself as a staff software engineer at Netflix in the AI platform org building large-scale distributed systems for ML model hosting. He frames the talk as a practitioner's playbook for using AI agents to improve performance engineering throughput and reduce infrastructure cost.

sections.title: The problem: fast code vs performant code
sections.summary: Coding agents produce code roughly 10x faster but don't always write the fastest code because they lack platform-specific knowledge and may invent new patterns. Compute costs rise alongside code production speed, creating a performance engineering gap in the new AI-assisted coding era.

sections.title: The manual profiling loop today
sections.summary: A human performance engineer triggers profiling on a production instance, downloads JSON call stack data, opens it in a visualizer, spends significant time hunting for bottlenecks, searches the codebase for potential improvements, produces a code review, and repeats. This is tedious and rarely done—profiling is typically only examined during 2 a.m. emergencies.

sections.title: The experiment: can an LLM read a profile?
sections.summary: The team asked whether an LLM could read profiling data faster than a human. Two assumptions: (1) all profilers speak the same language—structured call stack data with self/inclusive CPU regardless of language or runtime; (2) LLMs trained on quality code recognize common anti-patterns like O(N²) loops, loop invariants, repeated allocation, and batching issues. The agent identified a quadratic algorithm from profiling data alone, without scanning the codebase first.

sections.title: From call stack to the exact method
sections.summary: Once the agent identifies a pattern from profiling data, it can do a code search to find the repo, check out the exact production commit, locate the method definition, skip internal library details, and trace the full call path. This structured information becomes powerful for producing fixes.

sections.title: First finding and cross-service pattern detection
sections.summary: First finding: an O(N²) quadratic pattern in a tensor merge method (immutable map copy) consuming 8.8% CPU—the agent checked out the repo, found the code, and sent a code review in under 5 minutes. Second benefit: the agent found a spectator-metrics counter allocation pattern repeated across 7 services via cross-repo search, with potential 0.5–4.6% CPU savings. The talk transitions to embedding this into the development cycle.

sections.title: Building a shared pattern catalog as long-term memory
sections.summary: LLMs have compact memory and lack the context a human performance engineer possesses. To address this, Shah proposes a centralized pattern/anti-pattern catalog stored as markdown files in a Git repo—intentionally not a vector database. A stateful catalog combined with a stateless LLM creates fleet-wide memory. The catalog should be central and ever-growing, not team-specific. Patterns like the O(N²) example are generalizable across languages and frameworks. The catalog can be bootstrapped from public sources like Jeff Dean's C++ optimization blog, PyTorch's torch fix repo, and internal performance playbooks.

sections.title: Catalog entry structure and confidence tracking
sections.summary: A catalog entry includes queryable hints for LLM agents, a list of symbols, services where the pattern was confirmed, and a confidence level that increases as more services validate it. Each entry documents both the anti-pattern and the good pattern. The growing confidence helps future agents decide whether a finding is worth sending for human review.

sections.title: Human approval and verification gate
sections.summary: Human approval remains intentionally required—the agent sends code reviews rather than pushing directly to production. Modifying running production code without business context or sufficient test coverage is risky. To reduce noise, the agent should run unit and integration tests ahead of time to verify functional correctness before requesting human attention.

sections.title: Canary validation on real traffic
sections.summary: Before a code review reaches a human, canary deployment serves as a prerequisite. A canary runs two machines—one with old code, one with new—receiving the same traffic for ~10 minutes, comparing CPU usage, latency, and error rates. If error rates increase, the agent sees a red signal and does not proceed. The mental model: profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, engineer makes the decision.

sections.title: Reactive vs proactive paths and shift-left strategy
sections.summary: The reactive path—fixing code already in production—is too late and risky. Shah advocates shifting left: using the growing pattern catalog, a reviewer agent can provide inline comments during code review. Shifting further left, the catalog can be fed directly into coding agents during code authoring so they write optimal code from the start. The catalog must be hierarchically structured and indexed to avoid filling agent context windows unnecessarily.

sections.title: Foundations must precede AI agents
sections.summary: Shah cautions against putting AI agents into every SDLC step without solid foundations. Test coverage must be rock solid, business logic well-encoded in tests, and canary automation must be in place. AI agents need only know how to invoke canaries and read reports. The pattern catalog in a Git repo is a foundational piece designed to be readable by both humans and coding agents.

sections.title: Takeaways, autonomy levels, and next steps
sections.summary: Shah reiterates that foundations—code, automation, integration points (profiling triggers, data download, canary validation)—must come before LLMs. The reactive path is the right starting point, gradually moving left toward proactive prevention. He presents a stepwise autonomy model: Level 0 is fully manual (hours finding problems, no LLM); Level 1 introduces an LLM for identification only; Level 2 (this talk's focus) adds orchestration with tools, integrations, harnesses, and hooks, enabling scheduled weekly runs to continuously identify newly introduced problems; Level 3 gives the agent capabilities to plan, reason, and act but requires heavy investment in evaluation, sandboxing, and security guardrails against prompt injection. He recommends starting at Level 1, moving to Level 2 for maximum benefit, and considering Level 3 only as needed. Humans can also author catalog patterns when building new frameworks.

demonstrations: Agent reading profiling data to identify a quadratic pattern (immutable map copy in tensor merge method) and producing a code review in under 5 minutes
Agent performing cross-repo code search to find the same spectator metrics counter allocation pattern across 7 different services
Agent checking out a Git repo at the exact production commit, locating the method definition, and tracing the full call path
Canary deployment comparing old vs new code on real traffic for ~10 minutes to validate CPU, latency, and error rate improvements before human review
Pattern catalog entry structure with hints, symbols, confirmed services, confidence levels, and anti-pattern/good-pattern pairs in a centralized Git repo
Stepwise autonomy model from Level 0 (manual) through Level 2 (orchestrated agent with tools and scheduled runs) to Level 3 (agent plans and reasons autonomously)

organization.name: Netflix
organization.summary: Netflix is a global streaming entertainment company (NASDAQ: NFLX) headquartered in Los Gatos, California, founded in 1997. The company operates a substantial AI Platform organization that builds ML infrastructure including model training, inference, feature stores, and agent platforms supporting recommendations, search, personalization, and studio applications. The talk's speaker, Rajat Shah, is a Staff Software Engineer in the AI Platform org at Netflix, where his team built an autonomous performance engineering agent that uses LLM-based coding agents to identify and fix performance inefficiencies in production services, achieving measurable CPU reductions validated through canary deployments. The Model Inference Platform that the agent targets serves over 1M requests per second as of 2025.

technologies.label: AI Agent Orchestration for Performance Engineering
technologies.primary: Agent orchestration with tool integration for performance engineering
technologies.summary: The talk's primary focus is an orchestrated agent architecture for performance engineering operating at Level 2 autonomy. The agent integrates profiling tools, Git repositories, cross-repo code search, and canary deployment into a closed loop: read structured profiling data, identify anti-patterns, locate source code at the exact production commit, produce fixes, and validate them via canary deployment. The full find-to-code-review cycle was demonstrated in under 5 minutes in a large codebase, identifying a quadratic-time pattern consuming 8.8% CPU and a cross-service pattern across 7 services with 0.5–4.6% potential CPU savings. Scheduled weekly runs enable continuous identification of newly introduced problems. The speaker recommends starting at Level 1 (LLM identification only) and moving to Level 2 for maximum benefit, with Level 3 (autonomous planning) requiring heavy security investment.
technologies.role: Core technology architecture presented and demonstrated throughout the talk—explicitly identified as 'this talk mainly covered the level two orchestration' with scheduled weekly runs, tool integrations, harnesses, and hooks

technologies.label: Performance Profiling and Call Stack Analysis
technologies.primary: Performance profiling with structured call stack data
technologies.summary: Performance profiling produces structured call stack data with self CPU and inclusive CPU metrics that is universally parseable across languages and runtimes. This is the foundational input to the agent pipeline—the speaker's first key assumption is that all profilers speak the same structured language, making automated LLM-based analysis viable. The talk's primary example is an O(N²) quadratic pattern (immutable map copy in a tensor merge method) consuming 8.8% of CPU, identified from profiling data alone without scanning the codebase first. Scheduled continuous profiling transforms profiling from a reactive incident-response tool (typically only examined during 2 a.m. emergencies) into a proactive continuous identification mechanism.
technologies.role: Foundational input technology—the speaker's first key assumption is that all profilers speak the same structured language, which makes the entire agent approach viable without language-specific tooling

technologies.label: Pattern Catalog as Long-term Agent Memory
technologies.primary: Centralized pattern catalog as long-term agent memory
technologies.summary: A centralized pattern/anti-pattern catalog stored as markdown files in a Git repo serves as long-term memory for stateless LLM agents, creating fleet-wide memory. The design intentionally avoids vector databases for simplicity and human-readability. Each catalog entry includes queryable hints for LLM agents, a list of symbols, services where the pattern was confirmed, confidence levels that increase with validation, and both anti-pattern and good-pattern examples. The catalog can be bootstrapped from public sources and authored by humans building new frameworks. The growing confidence helps future agents decide whether a finding is worth sending for human review, reducing false positives over time.
technologies.role: The memory architecture that solves the LLM compact memory limitation—the speaker describes it as 'long-term memory that it could reuse' and 'a stateful catalog combined with a stateless LLM creates fleet-wide memory'

technologies.label: Canary Deployment and Automated Validation
technologies.summary: Canary deployment serves as the prerequisite validation gate before human code review—comparing old vs new code on real production traffic for approximately 10 minutes across CPU usage, latency, and error rates. The mental model: profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, engineer makes the decision. If error rates increase, the agent sees a red signal and does not proceed. Netflix's Kayenta (co-developed with Google, integrated with Spinnaker) provides the automated canary analysis infrastructure. Solid test coverage is a hard prerequisite—unit and integration tests must verify functional correctness before canary validation is meaningful and optimization changes are safe to review.
